source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Immediate memory span is limited by number of items (chunks), not by bits of information. Absolute-judgment span is limited by bits (about 2.5 bits, about 6 to 7 categories).
numbers: Hayes: span about 9 for binary digits, about 5 for 1000 monosyllabic words. Judgment channel capacity about 2.5 bits for pitch, 2.3 loudness, 3.25 for position.
quote: the number of bits of information is constant for absolute judgment and the number of chunks of information is constant for immediate memory
limits: The word chunk is left loosely defined by Miller himself. Five words could also be called 15 phonemes. The seven is a rough range, not a fixed constant.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library should be sized in chunks, not tokens. Context cost per chunk should be flat; bits per chunk should grow.

source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Recoding raises span by grouping input and naming the group. Smith's binary-to-octal demonstration: span is a fixed number of chunks, so bigger chunks hold more bits.
numbers: 20 subjects: span 9 binary digits, 7 octal digits. Recoding schemes studied 5 to 10 min raised binary span less than octal span predicted. Smith drilled himself: 12 octal chunks worth 24 bits (2:1), 36 bits (3:1), about 40 bits (4:1 and 5:1).
quote: the translation from one code to the other must be almost automatic or the subject will lose part of the next group
limits: Recoding must be nearly automatic or the translation load eats the span. A few minutes of study was not enough for 4:1 and 5:1 ratios. Recoding schemes tested on only 5 subjects each.
agent_relevance: A named, well-learned subgoal compresses many steps into one slot. An unlearned or costly-to-expand name will not help; the expansion cost must be near zero.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess, Cognitive Psychology 4
finding: Original chess study: three players (master M, Class A player A, beginner B) in a perception task (copy with the model in view) and a 5 s memory task. Recall tracked playing strength for game positions but not for random ones.
numbers: Middle game, trial 1: M about 16 pieces, A about 8, B about 4. End game: M about 8, A about 7, B about 4. Random positions: no relation between skill and recall; all three did worse than B on game positions. Perfect reconstruction needed M 3 to 4 trials, B up to 14.
quote: In the random, unstructured positions there was no relation at all between memory of the position and playing strength.
limits: N = 3 subjects, and the master was inactive in chess at the time. Samples this small cannot show a small skill effect on random boards. De Groot's earlier masters recalled more than M.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the gain is domain structure, not general capacity. Test the library on structured and scrambled task sets as the control.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess, Cognitive Psychology 4
finding: Chunk boundaries can be found from timing. Pieces placed within one glance came less than 2 s apart; between glances in the copy task the gap was about 3 s. Pauses of more than 2 s mark chunk boundaries.
numbers: Between-glance mean latency 2.8 s (M), 3.2 s (A), 3.5 s (B), p < .05. About 2 s to start a chunk plus about 300 ms per element to move it into short-term memory. Within-chunk pieces share chess relations (attack, defense, proximity, same colour, same type); between-chunk pairs look like chance. Subject-to-subject correlations of relation profiles about .91 to .95.
limits: The boundary is a 2 s cutoff chosen from the data. Pieces placed one by one may be guesses, not chunks. Hand movement time adds noise.
agent_relevance: A chunk is something retrieved as one act, which we can detect by latency or shared relations. For our library, a chunk test could be: do its steps always co-occur and get used together.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess, Cognitive Psychology 4
finding: Master recalled both more chunks and larger chunks than weaker players. Chunks recalled early are bigger than chunks recalled later.
numbers: First chunk recalled: master 3.8 pieces, Class A 2.6, beginner 2.4 (as cited by Gobet and Simon 1998). Number of chunks per position inside the 7 plus or minus 2 range but rising with skill, which the theory had not predicted.
quote: Taken at face value, these data suggest that M achieves his superior performance by recalling both more chunks and larger chunks.
limits: The prediction that chunk count would be constant across skill failed. The authors called the result surprising.
agent_relevance: Both library breadth (more chunks) and chunk size matter. Do not assume only size grows with skill.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Skill in chess, American Scientist 61
finding: Popular summary of the chunking theory with the standard numbers: masters and grandmasters reproduce about 25-piece positions at about 93%; experts about 72%; Class A about half; novices about 8 pieces (33%). With random positions all players recalled only 3 to 4 pieces.
numbers: 93% master and grandmaster, 72% expert, about 50% Class A, 33% (about 8 pieces) novice. Random boards: about 3 to 4 pieces for every level. First-chunk size 3.8 (master) vs 2.6 (Class A); chunks per position 7.7 vs 5.7. 77 chunks in one master's protocol: 47 pawn chains, 10 castled king positions, 27 other same-colour clusters (75% highly stereotyped).
limits: American Scientist version, written for a general audience. Figures come from a few subjects. The authors flag the chunk-count discrepancy as an open problem.
agent_relevance: Chunks in expert domains are common recurring patterns, not odd ones. A library should be built from patterns that recur often.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Skill in chess, American Scientist 61
finding: Three-part theory: (1) short-term memory of about seven chunk names, (2) a large long-term store of familiar patterns reached through an EPAM discrimination net, (3) a learning process that builds chunks at about 5 s per chunk. If one piece were a chunk a player could hold about seven; recalling over 20 pieces implies chunks of about 3 pieces on average.
numbers: Learning time about 5 s per new chunk in this article (later CHREST work uses 8 s to create a node and about 1 s to add to an existing node). Chunk vocabulary estimated at about 50,000 patterns, matched to a reading vocabulary of 50,000 words. Estimated 10,000 to 50,000 hours of looking at positions for a master, 1,000 to 5,000 for Class A.
limits: The 50,000 estimate was a crude extrapolation from a small simulation net (about 1,000 patterns) and an assumed word-like frequency distribution.
agent_relevance: Gives numeric priors for our design: tens of thousands of patterns, years of experience, a few seconds per new entry. Library growth needs a long run of examples.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Skill in chess, American Scientist 61
finding: MAPP and PERCEIVER: Simon and Chase built a program (MAPP) combining a simplified PERCEIVER (eye-movement scan driven by attack and defense relations) with a simplified EPAM net. It reconstructs boards from chunks.
numbers: With about 1,000 patterns MAPP performed about like a Class A player, twice a beginner, half a master. It recalled 51% of pieces the master placed correctly and 30% of pieces the master missed. Within-chunk relations like humans; between-chunk relations near random.
limits: 1,000-pattern net only. Gobet (1998) says most attacks on the chunking theory were aimed at MAPP, which implemented only part of the theory.
agent_relevance: An explicit, runnable computer model of a chunk library is the right form for a theory; compare with our code-checked library.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Multiple-board recall: players recalled up to five briefly shown positions. Percent recalled falls as boards increase but total pieces recalled rises past the seven-chunk limit for strong players.
numbers: Exp 1: 13 subjects (3 masters mean Elo 2453, 4 experts 2180, 6 Class A 1883), 5 s per board, 1 to 5 boards. Some subjects exceeded 7 plus or minus 2 chunks, up to 15 chunks. Serial position curve was U-shaped.
limits: Presentation order always went from 1 to 5 boards, so fatigue could confound; mouse and screen interface. Masters' largest chunks were bigger with one board than with several.
agent_relevance: Short-term chunk count alone does not explain strong performers. A fixed 7-slot plan underrates what a good library can hold.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Longer gaps between boards help recall, because new chunks or slots are being written to long-term memory. Masters gain more than experts.
numbers: Exp 2: 5 subjects (1 grandmaster, 1 IM, 1 master, 2 experts); gaps 1, 2, 5, 10 s. One game board: masters 92.3%, experts 64.5%. One random board: masters 21.1%, experts 17.7%. Gain from 1 to 10 s gap: masters +71% (2 boards) and +63% (4 boards); experts +40% and +33%. At 10 s with 4 boards (100 pieces) masters placed 82.9, experts 44.9.
limits: N = 5. No serial-position effect pooled (47.6 to 51.1% across 4 boards); masters showed a non-significant U shape.
agent_relevance: Time to consolidate into the library matters. A scaffold step that stores a new pattern needs budget; do not expect immediate reuse.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Trained master pushed multi-board recall with a retrieval structure. Over many sessions one Master (Elo about 2396) learned a cue list of world-champion names to tag each board.
numbers: Exp 3: baseline without cue list 50 and 55% on four boards, 54.3% on five boards (68 pieces). Peak of nine boards in block 18 above the 60% criterion; average 8 boards in blocks 19 to 22, then 7 boards. Percent correct rose linearly: 54.97 + 0.71 per block (r2 = .51) for n boards; 71.82 + 0.58 per block (r2 = .68) for two boards. Gobet (1998) cites up to 160 pieces replaced correctly.
limits: Single subject who collaborated with the experimenters; slightly weaker than the best master of Cooke et al. (1993, who claimed 9 boards). The Cooke claim of 9 boards was judged dubious by the authors because percent correct fell with board number.
agent_relevance: A cue list (retrieval structure) multiplies capacity but needs deliberate training; an index plus chunks beats chunks alone.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Template theory: besides fixed chunks, long-term memory holds templates, which are core patterns of about a dozen pieces with slots (variables, some with default values) that can be filled in about 1 to 2 s. Templates are built implicitly from many games; retrieval structures are built on purpose.
numbers: Chunks: up to 5 or more pieces. Templates: about 12 fixed pieces plus slots. Slot fill time about 1 to 2 s versus about 8 s to build a new chunk.
quote: The main novelty of this theory is the hypothesis that ... there are chunks (retrieval structures and templates) in long-term memory that contain variables (slots)
limits: A theory proposal. Later CHREST versions add template-creation and link mechanisms. Slot sizes and default values were not tested directly in this paper.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue for our schema: a subgoal template with slots and defaults, instantiated from the task, not fixed text. Cheap to instantiate, expensive to create.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Prior evidence against the pure short-term chunk model (interference tasks). Chess recall barely drops after an interrupting task.
numbers: Charness (1976): a 30 s delay with or without interfering task cut recall only 6 to 8% (versus large drops for trigrams) but delayed the first piece. Frey and Adesman (1976): two boards 8 s each then 3 or 30 s of counting; small loss. Saariluoma (1989): grandmasters encode up to four positions at 2 s per piece.
limits: Gobet and Simon argue the original model fits Frey and Adesman once learning time per chunk and long exposure are counted. Level-of-processing studies confounded depth with presentation time.
agent_relevance: Memory for domain material is stored durably, not held in a small buffer. The scaffold should store compiled results, not carry them in context.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories, Cognition 66
finding: Compares four theories on chess memory data: chunking (Chase and Simon), SEEK (Holding), long-term working memory (Ericsson and Kintsch), template theory. Chunking does better than usually stated; template theory fits best.
numbers: Discriminating areas: random and distorted positions, very short presentation, interference. Ellis (1973): at 150 ms, class A kept 6.7 of 8 pieces vs 4.5 for class D and below. Gobet and Simon (1995): masters placed about 70% of 26 pieces after 1 s, close to 90% after longer exposure.
quote: Contrary to recurrent criticisms in the literature, it is shown that the chunking theory is consistent with most of the data.
limits: Review, not a new experiment. The author also built the template theory, so the ranking is not independent. Verbal theories (SEEK, LT-WM) were judged too vague to refute.
agent_relevance: Use a computable model to compare competing library designs. Vague hypotheses cannot be ablated.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories, Cognition 66
finding: Random positions: skill effect exists but is small. Gobet and Simon pooled a dozen or so studies (presentation 10 s or less). Chase and Simon's 1973 master did worse than the novice, the one exception.
numbers: Masters placed about 5.5 pieces vs 2.6 for players below class B (5 s random positions). Gobet and Simon (1995): with 20 subjects over 1 to 60 s, recall growth fit an exponential function, r2 > .90; at 1 min masters placed about 17 of 26 random pieces (68%). Saariluoma (1991): masters recalled random legal move sequences almost perfectly after 15 moves; random illegal sequences under 20%.
limits: Most single studies had too little power; the effect was rarely significant on its own. Holding and Reynolds (1982) found no correlation of skill (Elo 1000 to 2200) with random-position recall.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a scrambled control to rule out skill effects; random boards still contain accidental small chunks.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories, Cognition 66
finding: Long-term working memory and skilled-memory theory: retrieval structures, elaborated cues, practice-speeded retrieval. The S.F. and D.D. digit-span data are the base for it. A retrieval structure applies to one kind of material only, with no transfer.
numbers: Three principles: encoding with elaborated cues tied to prior knowledge; encoding and retrieval time falls with practice; retrieval structures. The LT-WM square-board version predicts a skill effect on random positions much stronger than found.
limits: Gobet's judgment, as proponent of an alternative.
agent_relevance: Retrieval structures do not transfer across material types; build one per task family.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis, Memory 6
finding: Replication of Chase and Simon's copy and recall tasks (computer version). The 2 s chunk boundary replicated; profiles of chess relations correlate highly with the 1973 data.
numbers: 26 male subjects: 5 masters (Elo 2453), 9 experts (2148), 12 Class A (1869). Copy task: 79.5% of within-glance latencies under 2 s vs 1.11% of between-glance latencies; 89.3% vs 4.4% under 2.5 s. Between-glance median 7.3 s (longer than Chase and Simon's mean about 3 s). Recall task: 18.6 relations vs 1.3 for pairs under 2 s vs over 2 s.
quote: The 2-second inter-chunk interval used to define chunk boundaries is robust, and that chunks have psychological reality.
limits: Computer mouse and screen differ from physical pieces; latencies somewhat slower. One master viewed the board only once before copying.
agent_relevance: Chunk boundaries are measurable and reproducible across 25 years; timing-based chunk detection can be used for logging an agent's steps.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis, Memory 6
finding: Departure from the original: chunk size. With the 2 s cutoff the largest chunk was much larger than Chase and Simon found, which motivated templates.
numbers: Original: master first chunk 3.8, class A 2.6, beginner 2.4; median largest chunk about 5 pieces for the master. New study: size of largest chunk varied with skill, F(2,23) = 11.81, p < .001; Gobet (1998) cites chunks up to 15 pieces for masters. Number of references back to the stimulus: Skill F(2,23) = 8.31, p = .002.
limits: Differences may come from strategy, method, interface or the original's small hand-held batches of pieces. The authors list reasons rather than test them.
agent_relevance: Chunk size is not fixed at 3 to 4; with a good schema, big chunks exist. Estimate size per agent, not assumed.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions, Memory & Cognition 24
finding: Chunks are location-specific. Mirror-reflecting a game position about the vertical or central axis hurts recall, more than reflecting about the horizontal axis, but still beats random positions.
numbers: Exp 2 (26 subjects, Masters, Experts, Class A). Normal and horizontal pooled: 77.3% (masters), 49.7% (experts), 34.5% (Class A); vertical and central pooled 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Skill x position type interaction F(2,22) = 3.48, p < .05. Chunks per position 4.0 / 4.3 / 2.5 (game) vs 1.2 / 1.7 / 1.8 (random) for masters / experts / Class A. Omission errors on random boards 19.0, 16.1, 17.9.
limits: Most kings sit on the king's side (about 82 to 85%), so vertical and central reflection also breaks usual placement priors. Effect is modest.
agent_relevance: A stored pattern is tied to its context. A subgoal learned in one task layout may not fire in another; test with a perturbed version of the task.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions, Memory & Cognition 24
finding: CHREST simulation: recall rises with the number of nodes in the discrimination net; the same net shows the mirror-image cost, matching humans. Bigger nets also recall random boards a little better.
numbers: Simplified CHREST, 14 nets of varying size, learning from several thousand grandmaster positions, 50 test positions in 4 permutations. Normal vs horizontal 65.4% vs 63.2% (F(1,13) = 19.80, p < .005). Normal and horizontal pooled vs vertical and central: F(1,13) = 363.92. Supports the order of magnitude of 50,000 chunks.
limits: Simplified model; the human impairment was small. Estimates are order of magnitude only.
agent_relevance: A runnable chunk model gave quantitative predictions that matched an experiment; a standard for our library tests.

source: Gobet (1998) Memory for the meaningless: how chunks help, CogSci 20
finding: CHREST (Chunk Hierarchy and REtrieval STructure) is an EPAM-family program. It has eye-movement perception, a discrimination net, a visual short-term memory of about 2 to 5 chunks, node learning, and templates and links.
numbers: Parameters from EPAM: 8 s to create a chunk in long-term memory, 4 s to flag a node, 50 ms to place a symbol in STM, 50 ms to compare two symbols, 10 ms per net test. Nets of 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 nodes, STM span 2 to 5. With span 4, random-position recall 10.5%, 15.6%, 20.3% for 1k, 10k, 100k nets; humans (class A, experts, masters; 10 s or less) 11.7%, 17.0%, 23.7%.
quote: They also corroborate earlier estimates that visual short-term memory may contain three or four chunks.
limits: Largest chunk in the program slightly smaller than in humans. Class A and expert models slightly below humans at 1 and 2 s. Correlation of STM span with largest chunk size low (0.20, 0.27, 0.03).
agent_relevance: CHREST is a concrete model; its best-fit STM of 3 to 4 chunks matches Cowan. Our agent's working buffer can be sized about 4 slots.

source: Gobet (1998) Memory for the meaningless: how chunks help, CogSci 20
finding: Time-course of recall of random boards. 20 subjects (5 grand or international masters Elo 2498, 8 experts 2121, 7 class A 1879) saw random positions for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 30 or 60 s. Recall followed an exponential curve; stronger players start higher at 1 s and gain more from extra time.
numbers: Pooled recall at 10 s or less: class A 11.7%, experts 17.0%, masters 23.7%. Masters reached about 68% (17 of 26) on random boards at 60 s (cited in Gobet 1998).
limits: One position per time per subject; small sample. Unclear whether the extra-time advantage is faster learning of new chunks or recognising more chunks.
agent_relevance: Skill advantage on unstructured material is real but small; deeper study time lets chunks form even on scrambled material.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of 28 samples (24 studies, 903 participants) of expert recall of random domain material: a reliable but moderate skill effect, not chess-specific. Matches chunking predictions.
numbers: Overall r = .41, 95% CI [.29, .51], I2 = 63%. After trim-and-fill for publication bias r = .29 [.17, .41]. By domain: games r = .42 (k = 11), music .69 (k = 5), programming .36 (k = 6), sports .30 [-.04, .58] (k = 3). Time of exposure not a significant moderator, Q(1) = 0.89. Binomial set: 45 studies, 1,401 participants, 55 samples.
limits: Publication bias (eight studies filled in); music effect likely reflects less random material. Reliability not corrected (only 5 studies gave reliabilities).
agent_relevance: Skill effects on scrambled material are the signature of chunk-based, not schema-based, memory. A scrambled-task control should still show small library gains.

source: Cowan (2010) The magical mystery four, Curr Dir Psychol Sci
finding: Short-term capacity is closer to 3 to 5 chunks than Miller's 7; learned multi-item chunks occupy a slot like single items.
numbers: Chen and Cowan: about 3 chunks recalled whether items were singletons or learned word pairs. Saults and Cowan: about 4 items, visual and auditory pooled. Young adults: 3 to 5 meaningful items.
quote: a central memory store limited to 3 to 5 meaningful items in young adults
limits: Review of the capacity-limit view (Cowan 2001 BBS). Contested; rehearsal and grouping can inflate span, which is Miller's seven.
agent_relevance: Work with a buffer of about 4 slot chunks. A bigger context helps only if it holds learned units.

source: Wikipedia: Chunking (psychology)
finding: Secondary summary of Ericsson, Chase and Faloon (1980) S.F. study: normal digit span of 7 rose to almost 80 digits using mnemonic associations (running times, ages, dates), not a larger short-term buffer.
numbers: Span 7 to almost 80 digits in about 230 hours (about 20 months); chunks of 3 to 4 digits, never more than 6 digits rehearsed. Other summaries (not opened): running times 62% and ages 25% of his codes; a later report says about 80 digits after 250 hours.
limits: Source is Wikipedia, so numbers are second-hand; the primary paper (Science 208:1181) was blocked (403). Single subject; S.F. was a keen runner.
agent_relevance: Skill came from a chunk vocabulary plus a retrieval structure. For our agent: familiar units plus a deliberate index, built over many hours of practice.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Gobet and Simon (1996) Appendix 2 contrasts the S.F. and D.D. digit retrieval structures with chess templates. Digit structures were tree-like with 3 to 4 digits per twig; chunks were running times and ages. Chess templates are networks acquired as a by-product of play, not deliberately.
numbers: Both: rapid slot filling, long construction time (years), information stored in long-term memory. D.D.'s structure was built on purpose; chess templates are not. Templates contain default values and point to other templates (openings, endings).
limits: Qualitative comparison from the authors' table, no new data.
agent_relevance: Two designs for a library: arbitrary index (digit tree) vs content-based network (template). Our subgoal library is closer to the network type.
